title: Mark, Don't Erase: Token Inoculation for Dual-Use Knowledge in LLMs
topic: Social Aspects->Fairness, Equity, Justice and Safety
claim: Conditioning on a marker token, rather than suppressing content, gives selective refusal and a better safety-utility trade-off than baselines.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right; approach contrast, 3-step pipeline, Pareto scatter plot
description: A three-column figure split by dashed vertical lines. The left column, titled 'Dual-Use Domain' (e.g. clinical virology vs. viral manipulation), stacks three robot icons with arrows to outcomes. A robot trained to refuse gives Over-Refusal. A robot trained to unlearn gives Utility Trade-Off. A robot trained to refuse and to predict hazardous answers gives Selective Refusal, highlighted in orange. The middle column has three numbered stages. Continued pre-training shows a document with an inoculation token tag on a pink hazardous line. Supervised fine-tuning shows a user question branching to a refusal reply and a dashed-border reply with the token. Test-time shows a public user on a closed API who never receives the token. The right column is a scatter plot of MMLU accuracy against WMDP-Bio accuracy. Red stars forming a dashed Pareto frontier sit above the baseline markers. A legend is below the plot.
caption: Overview of Token Inoculation. Left: three ways to train on a dual-use domain. Refusal training over-refuses and unlearning trades away utility, while training to refuse and, on the same question, to predict the hazardous answer gives selective refusal. Middle: during continued pretraining, <|ino|> is prepended to the hazardous sentences of the corpus. During supervised finetuning the same question is answered with <|ino|> present and refused without it. In deployment the token is never issued to a public API user. Right: the safety-utility trade-off against unlearning and refusal baselines, with utility as the average of MMLU-Biology, MMLU-Virology, and MMLU- NonSTEM.
abstract: In a dual-use field, hazardous knowledge and the benign expertise around it share vocabulary, concepts, and causal structure. That overlap makes selective refusal hard, and existing methods such as unlearning and refusal training overgeneralize their suppression into the benign side. We argue for conditioning, not suppression. In this work, we introduce Token Inoculation, which marks hazardous sentences with a special token, the inoculation token, during continued pre-training. We then fine-tune the model to refuse hazardous questions and, on the same questions under the inoculation token, to predict the hazardous answers. At test time the inoculation token is absent, so the model does not express the hazardous answers it learned to predict. Across 1.5B to 14B parameters and three architecture families it holds hazardous accuracy near 18% while retaining 93% of the instruct baseline's MMLU performance, the best safety-utility balance among the baselines we compare. The same advantage reproduces under open-ended generation and in a cybersecurity transfer. We test this with a causal do(X) analysis that randomizes the accuracy of the conditioning signal, and find that refusal becomes more selective the more of the hazardous domain the model still knows. Our findings underscore the importance of training to predict the responses that must be refused, and outline a direction for safety alignment that does not degrade models' growing frontier knowledge. Project page: https://token-inoculation.github.io/
